title: How to Focus on What Actually Matters
author: Elevated Path
summary: Elevated Path argues that most people do not have a productivity problem but a priority problem, because too many worthwhile goals compete for the same limited attention. The piece retells the story, attributed to Warren Buffett's pilot Mike Flint, of the 25/5 exercise in which you write 25 goals, circle the top 5, and treat the other 20 as an avoid-at-all-costs list until the top 5 are done. The author claims the most dangerous distractions are not social media but good things we care about, and that working a little on everything feels productive while finishing nothing. He adds that unfinished tasks keep occupying mental attention, so open loops make focus harder. To choose the top 5 he suggests asking which goal has the biggest long-term payoff, which would make other goals easier, and which you would regret not pursuing. The practical close is a Not-Now List, framed as a decision about sequence rather than a rejection, and the piece includes a promotion for the author's paid framework playbook.
points: The 25/5 exercise forces a trade-off by splitting goals into a protected top 5 and an avoid-for-now list of 20, which treats the second list as a threat to focus rather than as a second priority.
Good goals are more dangerous than obvious distractions because each one comes with a reasonable excuse, so attention gets divided across many worthy projects.
The author separates motion from progress: touching every goal a little produces a busy week with nothing finished, whereas progress means keeping effort on one important thing.
Choosing a top 5 should use better questions than urgency, such as long-term payoff, whether a goal makes others easier, and whether you would regret skipping it.
A Not-Now List reframes declined goals as a matter of sequence, not never, which lowers the emotional cost of saying no.
quotes: You don’t have a productivity problem. You have a priority problem. You have too many things you want to do.
The other 20 weren’t his second priority. They were his avoid-at-all-costs list until the top 5 were accomplished.
But those aren’t always your most dangerous distractions. Sometimes your biggest distractions are good things.
Motion feels productive because you’re doing things. Progress happens when your effort keeps moving something important forward.
Because choosing one goal doesn’t just mean saying yes to it. It means saying not now to something else.
Your brain doesn’t only deal with what you’re doing. It also keeps track of what you’ve left open.
Not now” is not the same as “never.” It is a decision about sequence. And sequence matters.
Because you probably don’t need another productivity hack. You need the courage to care about fewer things at the same time.
